title: Tasks taking too long after updating to Airflow 2.7.0
body: Right after updating from Airflow 2.6.3 to 2.7.0, tasks that used to take about 15 seconds began taking around 10 minutes. More tasks were being queued than completed. We saw this across three projects: two Kubernetes instances and one Docker deployment. In the Docker Compose deployment, the only active DAG had at most four runs, no recently added high-resource DAGs, and used CeleryExecutor. Tasks remained queued for roughly two minutes and then took several more minutes while running. Downgrading that deployment to 2.6.3 made task timing look normal again.

symptoms_visible: After moving from Airflow 2.6.3 to 2.7.0, tasks that previously took about 15 seconds took around 10 minutes, with more tasks entering the queue than finishing.
Tasks stayed queued for about two minutes before starting and then took several more minutes to finish; after downgrading to 2.6.3, their timing looked normal again.
N0.label: N0 Airflow 2.7.0 slowdown reported after downgrade

symptoms_visible: For the same task, my 2.7.0 log has roughly 29-second pauses between the subtask line, the task-command line, and exporting environment variables; the corresponding 2.6.3 lines occur within about one second.
N1.label: N1 version-comparison logs collected

symptoms_visible: On another affected deployment, DAG runs increased from about 2.5 minutes to about 24 minutes after changing only Airflow from 2.6.3 to 2.7.0, and runs scheduled every 20 minutes began being skipped.
That deployment showed considerably more loopback traffic, and its debug task log repeatedly paused for several seconds between internal task-runner steps.
N2.label: N2 slowdown reproduced in another unchanged environment

symptoms_visible: With a one-minute DAG and about 28,000 retained dag_run rows, I saw each running DAG run repeatedly request all earlier successful runs; pending requests accumulated and other DAGs slowed as well.
N3.label: N3 repeated DAG history query captured

symptoms_visible: After updating to the maintenance build containing the query fix, task performance returned to its previous level and the long queued and execution delays no longer occurred.
N_terminal.label: N_terminal affected deployments confirm normal performance

question_patterns: Can you share logs for the same task on 2.6.3 and 2.7.0 so we can compare where the time is spent?
Do the task logs show a specific stage where execution pauses?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: For fetch_header on 2.7.0, the log goes from `Job 1180119: Subtask fetch_header` at 18:23:04 to `Running <TaskInstance...>` at 18:23:35, then to `Exporting env vars` at 18:24:06. In 2.6.3, those corresponding lines are at 19:28:45, 19:28:45, and 19:28:46. Every task also sat queued for about two minutes before it began.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The framework log lines are immediate in both versions; all of the extra time is inside my PythonOperator after my own code begins.
The same pauses are present, but they are around 20 seconds rather than 29 seconds.

edges.comment: Messages c1-c5, primarily jaetma's affected Docker/Celery deployment: potiuk requested comparable task logs, jaetma supplied raw 2.6.3 and 2.7.0 timestamps and clarified the queued delay. The conclusion about which internal phase is responsible remains engineer-side.

question_patterns: Can another affected operator describe the before-and-after task duration and what changed during the upgrade?
Can you reproduce the slowdown in an environment where the Airflow version is the only changed component?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: In our deployment, DAG runs averaged about 2.5 minutes before the 2.7.0 update and about 24 minutes afterward. The DAG runs every 20 minutes, so Airflow started skipping runs. We also saw considerably more traffic over the loopback interface.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: We changed Airflow, Python, the database host, and machine sizing together, and cannot reproduce the slowdown when only Airflow changes.
The task duration rose from three minutes to about 22 minutes, with the same loopback-traffic increase.

question_patterns: What is the affected deployment, Python version, and database, and did any of those change?
Please summarize the environment where you reproduced the slowdown.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: We changed Airflow from 2.6.3 to 2.7.0 without changing Python. Our .pex files use Python 3.9. Airflow runs on three RHEL 8 VM hosts and uses a local PostgreSQL 12 database; deployment is handled through Ansible.

question_patterns: Can you enable DEBUG logging and share a task log from an affected 2.7.0 run?
Please capture debug-level task logs so we can see where the pauses occur.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With logging_level=DEBUG on 2.7.0, my task log shows `previous_execution_date was called` at 14:23:49, `Loading core task runner` at 14:23:54, another `previous_execution_date was called` at 14:23:58, and `Planning to run` plus the TaskInstance refresh at 14:24:02. Similar multi-second gaps continue through the task startup log.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The debug log advances continuously through Airflow startup and pauses only after the external CLI starts.

edges.comment: Messages c25-c27 and c30-c35 describe Github-dm-CDE's separate RHEL/.pex deployment, folded into the simulated user side as corroborating affected-user evidence. The screenshots were originally supplied with that operator's timing and loopback observations. This deployment is not substituted for jaetma's Docker setup; it establishes that the same 2.7.0 symptom occurs when Python and infrastructure remain unchanged.

question_patterns: Can you paste the exact database query that accumulates while the affected DAG is running?
Which SQL statement is repeatedly requesting the DAG's history?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: For a run scheduled at 12:50, I captured this query: `SELECT dag_run.state, dag_run.id, dag_run.dag_id, dag_run.queued_at, dag_run.execution_date, dag_run.start_date, dag_run.end_date, dag_run.run_id, dag_run.creating_job_id, dag_run.external_trigger, dag_run.run_type, dag_run.conf, dag_run.data_interval_start, dag_run.data_interval_end, dag_run.last_scheduling_decision, dag_run.dag_hash, dag_run.log_template_id, dag_run.updated_at FROM dag_run WHERE dag_run.dag_id = 'patient_lists' AND dag_run.execution_date < '2023-08-31T12:40:00+00:00'::timestamptz AND dag_run.state = 'success' ORDER BY dag_run.execution_date DESC`. My one-minute DAG had about 28,000 dag_run rows retained, and I saw running DAG runs issue this history request repeatedly.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The accumulating SQL is unrelated to dag_run history and instead waits on an external application table modified by my task.
The same statement is captured for a ten-minute DAG with about 3,000 retained rows instead of the one-minute DAG.
The affected DAG has a different name, but the query shape and absence of a result limit are unchanged.

edges.comment: Messages c36-c40 describe nick-msk-ai's deployment, folded as a third affected operator in the same 2.7.0 diagnostic chain. c36 supplied the observed repeated history requests and row counts; c37 explicitly requested the exact query; c38 supplied the raw SQL. Taragolis then stated that this query was fixed. The identification of this behavior as the accepted Airflow regression belongs to the consuming solution.

solution.intent: Update from Airflow 2.7.0 to a maintenance build containing the DAG-run history query fix, which prevents task startup from repeatedly loading an unbounded set of earlier successful DAG runs, and have affected operators verify their normal runtimes before closing the incident.
solution.concrete_example: The captured query orders every earlier successful dag_run without limiting the result, so high-frequency DAGs can repeatedly load large histories and congest the metadata database. Upgrade to Airflow 2.7.1, where that query was fixed, then rerun representative DAGs and compare their queue and execution times before declaring the problem resolved.
solution.inference_hint: The affected operator supplied the raw SQL, observed repeated requests, and reported dag_run row counts. Taragolis connected that SQL to the already-fixed Airflow query, and multiple affected operators later confirmed normal performance after updating. Concluding that the unbounded/repeated previous-successful-DagRun lookup is the accepted root cause is engineer-side inference, not wording that should be placed in the user's raw query answer.

edges.comment: Messages c40-c47 form the resolution: Taragolis identified the captured query as fixed; affected operators were asked to retest the maintenance release; LuisLarisch, CM000n, jaetma, and raphaelsimeon then reported restored performance. jaetma's confirmation covers an originally affected Kubernetes instance; the other confirmations are retained as folded corroboration. Later c48-c52 concern a different 2.7.2/MWAA problem that remained partially reproducible on 2.6.3 and is deliberately excluded from this resolved 2.7.0 chain.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause as Airflow 2.7.0 repeatedly executing an unbounded prior-successful-dag_run history query, which becomes expensive for DAGs with large histories and can create metadata-database backlog and task delays.
The diagnosis must be grounded in the version-comparison timestamps, debug startup gaps, repeated-query observation, retained dag_run volume, and the captured SQL without a result limit.
Must recommend updating to a build containing the DAG-run query fix rather than treating downgrade as the permanent resolution.
Must not settle on the earlier DNS, top-level DAG code, Python pickle, resource-limit, or _PIP_ADDITIONAL_REQUIREMENTS hypotheses; the thread did not validate those as the final cause.

Must ask affected users to rerun representative DAGs on a build containing the fix and compare queue and execution times before declaring the issue resolved; the graph surfaces confirmations that normal performance returned.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced Airflow operators and maintainers folded into one simulated user side. They can compare versions, provide DAG and deployment details, enable debug logging, inspect PostgreSQL activity, and paste exact SQL, but the final causal interpretation is left to maintainers.
persona_hint.communication_style: Collaborative and evidence-driven. Supplies long logs, configuration excerpts, timestamps, screenshots, and environment summaries; readily performs requested comparisons and reports concrete timing changes.
